pages.title: Home
pages.content:
Study Circle

Ask, answer, learn together.

A friendly forum for students and lifelong learners: subject rooms, study tips and exam prep, with tutors and peers who explain things kindly.

Join the circle
Browse subjects

Subject rooms

Find your subject.

Every room has volunteer tutors who check answers and keep threads helpful.

Mathematics

Algebra to calculus, proofs and practice problems.

Sciences

Biology, chemistry and physics questions.

Languages

Grammar help, conversation partners and resources.

Writing and Humanities

Essays, history and literature.

Exam Prep

Schedules, past papers and last-week nerves.

Study Tips

Notes, focus and memory techniques that work.

How it works

  1. Ask. Post your question in the right room and show what you tried.
  2. Discuss. Peers and tutors explain the method, not only the answer.
  3. Pay it forward. Once it clicks, help the next person who gets stuck.

A kind place to not know things yet.

We explain instead of judging, we show our working, and we never post answers to live exams.

Read the guidelines

pages.title: Community guidelines
pages.content:
Study Circle works because everyone follows a few simple guidelines. Moderators and tutors apply them kindly and consistently.

  1. Show your working. Share what you tried so helpers can see where you got stuck.
  2. Explain, do not just answer. Good replies teach the method, not only the result.
  3. Academic honesty. No answers to live exams or graded work, and no paid essay offers.
  4. Be patient and kind. Everyone was a beginner once. Assume good intent.
  5. Use a clear title. “Integration by parts: where does the minus sign go?” beats “help pls”.

Tutors and moderators

Tutors are volunteers with experience in a subject; moderators keep the rooms tidy and answer reports. Both are marked with a badge next to their name.

pages.title: About Study Circle
pages.content:
Study Circle is run by volunteer tutors, teachers and students who believe that explaining something is the best way to learn it.

Who we are

We started as a revision group in a school library. Today the circle welcomes secondary school students, university students and adults going back to learning.

  • Amira Haddad, mathematics teacher and moderator
  • Priya S., writing tutor and moderator

Get in touch

Want to become a tutor, suggest a subject room or report a problem? Write to the team at team@example.com.

topics.author: amira
topics.title: Welcome to Study Circle: how to ask a great question
topics.content:
Welcome! Before your first post, have a look at the community guidelines. The short version: show what you tried, use a clear title and be kind.

Tutors and moderators carry a badge. If a reply helped you, say so: it keeps volunteers going.

replies.author: kofi
replies.content: Thank you! I did not know about the tutor badges.

replies.author: tomas
replies.content: Great idea to ask people to show their working.

topics.author: tomas
topics.title: Back to learning at forty: hello!
topics.content: Hi everyone, I am learning German for a new job and I have not studied anything formally in twenty years. Nervous but excited.

replies.author: priya
replies.content: Welcome, Tomás! The Languages room has a weekly conversation thread.

replies.author: lena
replies.content: You are never too old. Good luck with the new job!

topics.author: kofi
topics.title: Integration by parts: where does the minus sign go?
topics.content: I am trying to integrate x·ex and I keep getting the sign wrong. I used u = x and dv = ex dx. Here is my working so far: I get x·ex + ex, but the answer key says x·ex − ex.

replies.author: amira
replies.content:
Nice working! The formula is ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. You found uv = x·ex correctly; the minus sign belongs in front of ∫ex dx, which gives −ex.

So the result is x·ex − ex + C. Try differentiating it to check.

replies.author: kofi
replies.content: Differentiated it and got x·ex back. It finally makes sense, thank you!

topics.author: lena
topics.title: What does a p-value actually tell me?
topics.content: Every textbook defines it differently and I still could not explain it to a friend. Can someone give an intuitive explanation?

replies.author: amira
replies.content: It is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

replies.author: ben
replies.content: The coin example helped me: flip a fair coin ten times and get ten heads. How surprised should you be? That surprise is the p-value.

topics.author: ben
topics.title: Titration lab report: how precise should my results be?
topics.content: My titres are 23.40, 23.45 and 23.35 cm³. Are these concordant, and how many significant figures should I report?

replies.author: amira
replies.content: They are within 0.10 cm³ of each other, so they are concordant. Report the mean to two decimal places, as your burette reads.

replies.author: ben
replies.content: Great, that matches what my lab partner said.

topics.author: tomas
topics.title: German cases: a trick for remembering the dative?
topics.content: I keep mixing up accusative and dative after prepositions. Is there a memory trick people use?

replies.author: priya
replies.content: Many learners memorise the dative-only prepositions as a rhythm: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu.

replies.author: lena
replies.content: Flashcards with a full example sentence helped me more than lists.

topics.author: priya
topics.title: Writing a thesis statement in one sentence
topics.content: A strong thesis makes a claim that someone could disagree with, and it tells the reader how you will support it. Post yours here and we will give friendly feedback.

replies.author: kofi
replies.content: Mine: social media changed how young people get news, because it replaced editors with algorithms. Too broad?

replies.author: priya
replies.content: Good start! Narrow it: which young people, which platforms, and what changed exactly?

topics.author: lena
topics.title: Pomodoro did not work for me. What did?
topics.content: Twenty-five minutes is too short for maths problems; I lose the thread every break. Has anyone found a rhythm that works better?

replies.author: ben
replies.content: I do fifty minutes on, ten off, and stop at a point where I know the next step.

replies.author: tomas
replies.content: Writing down the next step before a break was the game changer for me too.

topics.author: amira
topics.title: Build your revision timetable (template inside)
topics.content:
Six weeks before exams is a good time to plan. List your subjects, rate your confidence from one to five and give weaker topics more slots, but never zero for the strong ones.

Leave one free evening per week. Rest is part of the plan.

replies.author: kofi
replies.content: Rating my confidence first made it obvious where to spend time.

topics.author: kofi
topics.title: Exam in a week and I cannot focus
topics.content: My first exam is next Monday and my head is all over the place. Any advice for the last week?

replies.author: priya
replies.content: Switch from learning new things to practising past papers under timed conditions, and sleep. You have done the work.
